newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher in line with overseas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher in line with overseas.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Friday in line with overseas trends.
Treasury prices gained in overseas trade and European government debt markets also displayed a firmer tone.

Analysts said curve-flattening trades were the order of the day. The spread between two- and 30-year Treasury securities had narrowed to 70 basis points in early trade, down from 77 basis points at Wednesday's close on the eve of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before the Joint Economic Committee of Congress.
The flatter yield curve reflects the stronger expectation that the Fed will decide to raise interest rates at its March 25 policy meeting.
Shortly after the market opened, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 5/32 to 96 even, yielding 6.94 percent.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-10/32, yielding 6.25 percent.

"The European bond market which had been under pressure all week was more stable overnight," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "People are looking at the curve trade, with more interest at the long end than in the short."
The data calendar is light, with February import/export prices due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT and the Treasury's federal budget statement for February due at 1400 EST/1900 GMT.
"Neither of those are market movers," said Stiles.
Participants said trading on Friday was likely to be narrow ranged.
"It looks more like narrow ranged trading bias with resistance (on the June bond contract) at 109-08 above us and much bigger resistance at 109-25," said Stiles.
"We're working off some oversold conditions in the long end but we still have the supply coming and the Fed meeting so the market won't really be able to get going," said Stiles.
The Treasury will sell $17.25 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-making arm of the Federal Reserve, gathers on Tuesday and the group is widely expected to raise interest rates at that time.
Stiles said the market "pretty much reflects" the eventuality of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike.

"The market has gotten the hint that the Fed is going to do something on Tuesday and the debate is shifting to how far they will go," said Stiles. "The Fed isn't going to do 25 basis points and walk away. People will be asking when they'll tighten again and these questions will dog the market. If Fed funds are heading to six percent by the end of the year, what's the right place to buy two-years (at Tuesday's Treasury auction)?"

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were up four basis points to 5.24 percent, six-month bill rates were up three basis points to 5.34 percent and year bill rates were up two basis points to 5.52 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-9/32, yielding 6.27 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 98-18/32, yielding 6.59 percent. Ten-year notes were up 2/32 to 96-20/32, yielding 6.72 percent.
